section_title: What does the right hand of fellowship express?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 9 And recognizing the grace that I had been given, James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.

context_lines: This verse belongs to Paul’s account in [Galatians 2:6–10](https://thewayofscripture.com/passages/galatians-2-6-10.html). The Jerusalem leaders recognized the grace given to him and the work God was doing through his ministry.

Paul names James, Cephas and John as people regarded as pillars. They extended fellowship to Paul and Barnabas, recognizing their work among the Gentiles while continuing their own work among the circumcised.
The wider paragraph speaks of the same God at work through different workers and ends with a shared concern for the poor. Fellowship here has both a gospel foundation and practical responsibilities.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read the gesture as recognition of shared work in the gospel. [Wesley’s note on verse 9](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-epistle-to-the-galatians/) describes receiving Paul and Barnabas as fellow workers; the [USCCB note on verses 7–9](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/galatians/2) likewise connects the fellowship with recognition of Paul’s mission.
god_plan_lines: [Romans 15:25–27](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/15.htm) describes Gentile believers contributing to poor believers in Jerusalem. Paul connects their material help with the spiritual blessings they have shared.

That later collection gives practical expression to the fellowship recognized here. Different areas of ministry belong within a shared faith, and that relationship includes care for one another across the distance between communities.
current_position_lines: Our study [Who Shepherds the Church?](https://thewayofscripture.com/studies/who-shepherds-the-church.html), in its discussion of James, recognizes the real authority and standing he had among the Jerusalem believers. It reads that standing alongside the other leaders and the shared decision-making described in Acts 15 and 21. The study distinguishes recognized personal standing from a separate rank meant to be reproduced in every church.
